A science-based pathway for 100% renewable electricity by 2040 and an equitable, resilient, net-negative economy by 2050.

About this report

The State, renowned for its rich biodiversity and high human development, has set a transformative target of achieving 100% reliance on renewable energy (RE) by 2040 and carbon neutrality by 2050 (CN50). By pursuing these goals, Kerala aims to achieve net-zero emissions well ahead of India’s national 2070 target through a sustained energy transition and deep emission reductions across key emitting sectors, with natural carbon sinks playing a significant role in addressing residual emissions. Although the State currently maintains a comparatively low-emission profile, with per capita emissions of 0.64 tCO₂e compared to the national average of 2.46 tCO₂e, sustaining this advantage and progressing towards carbon neutrality will require a comprehensive and transformative decarbonisation pathway. In this context, the CN50 Pathway envisions a major transition from a thermal power import dependent energy system to a renewable energy architecture supported by large-scale energy storage, grid modernisation, and distributed clean energy systems.

Kerala Carbon Neutral Pathway

2021 · Energy

Emission profile

Gross and net pathways, implementation sensitivities, and the role of land and blue-carbon sinks.

Gross Greenhouse Gas Emissions: BAU and CN50 Pathways

Kerala's gross greenhouse gas emissions were 22.18 MtCO₂e in 2021. Under the BAU scenario, emissions increase to 26.70 MtCO₂e by 2030 and subsequently decline to 25.90 MtCO₂e in 2050, remaining 16.77% above the 2021 level. The energy sector accounts for 3.18 MtCO₂e, or 85.37%, of the net increase between 2021 and 2050. Within energy-sector emissions, transport contributes 63.2%, buildings 21.6%, and industry, including captive power, 14.5%. Under CN50, electrification, energy efficiency, fuel switching, renewable electricity and improved waste management reduce projected gross emissions in 2050 by 55.54% relative to BAU, to approximately 11.52 MtCO₂e.

Carbon neutrality remains achievable under alternative implementation conditions

The CN50 pathway combines measures across energy and non-energy sectors, including accelerated vehicle electrification, the adoption of electric cooking, industrial fuel switching, improved waste management and expansion of land-based carbon sinks. The modelled pathway reaches net-negative emissions before 2050. Sensitivity cases further indicate that the carbon-neutrality objective remains achievable when selected interventions are implemented more slowly or at a lower scale, although the year of achievement is delayed.

The sensitivity analysis highlights the importance of implementation pace. Slower electrification in transport and industry, or lower sequestration, delays the reduction in net emissions but does not reverse the overall pathway. For example, if transport electrification reaches only 50% of the level assumed under CN50, the net-negative milestone shifts from 2032 to around 2040. The result underlines the need for time-bound sectoral targets, regular progress reviews and corrective measures where deployment falls behind schedule.

Expanding natural carbon sinks strengthens Kerala's net-negative pathway

The carbon sequestration potential of Kerala is projected to increase from 14,626 ktCO₂e per year under the Business-as-Usual (BAU) scenario to 23,912 ktCO₂e per year under the Carbon Neutral 2050 (CN50) pathway through a set of integrated land-based and blue carbon interventions. A major component of this strategy is the expansion of social forestry and agroforestry across approximately 75% of the state's 841.16 sq. km of barren, wasteland and fallow land, equivalent to about 630.87 sq. km, which is expected to sequester around 694 ktCO₂e annually. Alongside this, restoring Kerala's mangrove ecosystems from the current 21.15 sq. km to 100.60 sq. km by 2050, supported by long-term conservation and management, could contribute an additional 1,237 ktCO₂e per year. Another key intervention focuses on improving the carbon stock density of existing forests through afforestation, assisted natural regeneration (ANR), and better forest management practices. These measures are expected to increase forest carbon stocks by nearly 40%, resulting in an estimated 7,354 ktCO₂e of additional carbon sequestration each year. Beyond enhancing carbon sinks, these interventions will also strengthen biodiversity, improve ecosystem resilience, support watershed functions, and deliver multiple ecological co-benefits. Together, these land and coastal ecosystem restoration measures provide a practical pathway to significantly increase Kerala's carbon sequestration capacity and support its long-term goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050.

Land-based and blue-carbon interventions are critical to achieving net-negative emissions

Kerala’s carbon-negative ambition depends equally on the expansion and restoration of natural carbon sinks across forests, degraded lands and coastal ecosystems.

Achieving net-negative emissions hinges on increasing carbon sequestration to 23.91 MtCO₂e by 2050 through improved carbon-stock density in existing forests; repurposing 75% of 841.16 sq. km of barren and fallow land for agroforestry and social forestry; and restoring coastal blue-carbon ecosystems. Mangrove cover is projected to expand from 21.15 sq. km to 100.06 sq. km, alongside the restoration of seagrasses, salt marshes and other wetlands. These measures can simultaneously enhance carbon removal, biodiversity, soil health, coastal resilience and community livelihoods.

Sustainable agriculture and waste management are also central to reducing Kerala’s non-CO₂ emissions.

Sustainable agriculture and livestock-management practices are projected to reduce agriculture-sector emissions by 22.70% by 2050. Comprehensive domestic wastewater treatment—including 194 MLD of additional centralised aerobic capacity and 176 new faecal-sludge treatment plants—together with industrial-effluent management based on zero liquid discharge and zero-landfill municipal-solid-waste management, is expected to reduce waste-sector emissions by approximately 78.81% by 2050. Together, these measures reduce projected non-energy emissions from 4.02 MtCO₂e under BAU to 1.72 MtCO₂e under CN50.

Technology transition

Electricity demand, economy-wide electrification, renewable capacity, storage and power-system transformation.

Electricity demand will increase nearly fivefold by 2050, requiring rapid renewable-capacity expansion

Economy-wide electrification increases Kerala's electricity demand to 123.70 TWh by 2050, nearly five times the 2021 level. Industry and transport account for a large share of the additional demand, while higher cooling requirements in buildings are partly moderated by energy-efficiency improvements. The modelling indicates that 65.06 GW of renewable-energy capacity will be required by 2050, including 50.52 GW of solar and 11.28 GW of wind. This expansion will need to combine continued rooftop-solar deployment with utility-scale renewable projects, adequate storage, grid strengthening and demand-side flexibility.

Electrification is the principal enabler of economy-wide decarbonisation

Under the CN50 scenario, electrification supports both emission reduction and energy-security objectives. Kerala's dependence on oil and gas exposes the economy to international price volatility, supply disruptions and geopolitical risks. Shifting transport, cooking and suitable industrial heat applications to domestically supplied renewable electricity reduces this exposure. The pathway assumes 100% electrification of new two- and three-wheeler sales by 2040, followed by near-complete electrification of passenger vehicles and light goods vehicles by 2050, while residual diesel use remains in heavy-duty freight. It also includes electric cookstoves across about 55 lakh households and commercial establishments and the electrification of industrial heat where technically feasible. Together, these measures could abate about 11.35 MtCO₂e annually by 2050.

Solar-led capacity expansion enables a low-carbon power system by 2050

By 2050, renewable energy, including large hydro, supplies more than 95% of electricity generation under both the BAU and CN50 scenarios. Solar is the largest source, accounting for about 69.8% of generation in BAU and 72.65% in CN50, while wind and hydropower provide additional supply diversity and system support. Thermal generation falls below 1% of total supply, and only a limited share is procured from inter-state markets. The grid emission factor consequently declines from about 0.58 kgCO₂/kWh in 2021 to near-zero levels by 2045 under BAU and by 2040 under CN50.

Modelling framework

TIMES optimises the economy-wide energy system; PyPSA tests power-system capacity, operation and reliability.

TIMES–PyPSA Energy Modelling Framework

The assessment combines the TIMES Kerala energy-system optimisation model, implemented through CPLEX and GAMS, with the PyPSA Kerala power-system planning model. Sector demand projections, resource availability, future technologies, policy objectives, operational constraints and sensitivity cases are linked to assess least-cost energy pathways and the electricity-system investments required to achieve Kerala's 2040 renewable-electricity and 2050 carbon-neutrality objectives.

Way forward

Implementation priorities, finance, institutional coordination and monitoring.

Implementation Priorities and Way Forward

Implementation of the CN50 pathway will require a whole-of-government approach, clear sectoral responsibilities and coordination across State departments, local governments, utilities, regulators, financial institutions and the private sector. The implementation framework should remain sufficiently flexible to incorporate changes in technology costs, market conditions and development priorities without weakening the long-term carbon-neutrality objective.

Sectoral departments should translate the pathway into time-bound action plans with defined targets, milestones, budgets and institutional responsibilities. These actions should be integrated into existing State and sector planning processes and, where relevant, into local-government development plans. A decentralised implementation model can support context-specific delivery, provided that all programmes follow a common monitoring and reporting framework.

Financing will require a combination of public expenditure, climate finance and private investment. Priority areas include mechanisms to reduce investment risk, improve access to concessional finance and support commercially viable low-carbon projects. Technology deployment should be supported by stronger linkages among research institutions, industry, utilities and implementing agencies, along with procurement, standards and capacity-building measures that facilitate the adoption of proven solutions.

A formal monitoring, reporting and review system should track sectoral emissions, energy demand, technology uptake, renewable capacity, sequestration outcomes and financial flows. Progress should be reviewed periodically against interim milestones, and assumptions should be updated to reflect technological, economic and policy developments. This process will enable timely corrective action and maintain alignment with the 2050 objective.
